observations.limitations: The passage identifies an eating utensil but does not describe its shape.
observations.observation: Advice about eating says people who struggle to use “sendok dan garpu” can have their hands guided toward the mouth.
observations.source_title: Masalah Gizi pada Lansia dan Cara Mengatasinya

observations.limitations: One edited source does not establish relative frequency against alternatives.
observations.observation: The guidance uses “sendok dan garpu” without explanation for utensils used to eat.
observations.source_title: Masalah Gizi pada Lansia dan Cara Mengatasinya

observations.limitations: The cited lead concerns measuring spoons, so it does not by itself establish the preferred name of an eating spoon.
observations.observation: The recipe repeatedly uses “sendok makan” and “sendok teh” as ingredient measures.

observations.limitations: The entry also lists unrelated senses; it does not rank “sudu” against “camca.”
observations.observation: Kamus Pelajar defines the utensil sense as a small tool used to scoop food and gives “camca” as a synonym.

observations.limitations: This is natural public usage, but no frequency comparison with “camca” was made.
observations.observation: The article uses “sudu dan garpu” for modern utensils used to bring food to the mouth.
observations.source_title: Adakah Kita Digalakkan untuk Menjilat Baki Makanan yang Melekat pada Sudu Selepas Makan?

observations.limitations: The examples establish natural choices in these contexts, not population-wide frequencies.
observations.observation: The Indonesian source uses “sendok” and the Malaysian source “sudu” in parallel eating-with-fork contexts.
observations.publisher: Kementerian Kesehatan Republik Indonesia; Jabatan Mufti Wilayah Persekutuan
